what does an ignition coil do
A misfire means one or more cylinders isn't burning fuel properly, which causes shaking, a rough idle, hesitation or loss of power.
Uneven idle, hesitation, shaking, reduced power, stalling, or a flashing malfunction indicator may occur.
what causes an engine to overheat
Overheating means the cooling system isn't removing heat fast enough, or coolant isn't circulating properly.
Overheating mainly at idle or in slow traffic, which improves once you're moving, points to too little airflow at low speed. Check that the cooling fan comes on before replacing parts.

Overheating at highway speed or when climbing or loaded can come from poor coolant flow, a partly blocked radiator, low coolant or the engine making extra heat. It doesn't point to one part on its own.
If the heater blows cold while the temperature gauge climbs, coolant may be low or not circulating. That is an urgent warning.

A sweet smell, wet spots, dried crusty residue, coolant that keeps dropping, or steam all suggest a coolant leak. No puddle doesn't rule one out: some leaks only happen when hot, or inside the engine.
A temperature that goes up and down, gurgling sounds, or recent cooling-system work can mean trapped air or low coolant, but it needs checking to be sure.
Persistent bubbles, rapid pressurization from a cold start, unexplained coolant loss, or white exhaust may warrant internal-leak tests; none alone proves a head-gasket failure.

A red oil-pressure warning means the engine may not be getting enough oil pressure, which can damage it within minutes. Leaks and oil burning lower the oil level more gradually.
Oil warning lamp, visible oil drops, smoke, burning-oil odor, or a level that repeatedly falls.

For most cars, change the engine oil and filter every 5,000 to 10,000 km or every 6 months, whichever comes first. City traffic, short trips and heat count as severe service, so for a car driven in Metro Manila plan on about every 5,000 km; go longer only if the owner's manual or the oil-life monitor allows it.
A service reminder or oil-life message should be interpreted using the owner's manual; an oil-pressure warning is a separate, more urgent condition.
Fuel delivery, air intake, sensors, and ignition
Fuel, air-intake, sensor and ignition problems can cause hard starting, hesitation, stalling or poor fuel economy.
Long cranking, rough running, hesitation, stalling, reduced power, or an engine warning light.
Timing belts, timing chains, and engine wear
A timing belt or chain keeps the engine's valves and pistons in step. If it slips or breaks, the engine stops and can be badly damaged.
Unusual noise from the timing area or the engine running badly is a reason to have it inspected, but symptoms alone can't tell how worn the belt or chain is.
Brake pads, rotors, calipers, and wear symptoms
how often should i change brake pads
when should i replace brake pads
how long do brake pads last
Brake pads and rotors wear with use. Squealing, grinding, vibration when braking or a longer stopping distance are signs they need inspecting.
Squealing, grinding, vibration while braking, pulling, longer stopping distance, or a changed pedal feel.
A squeak or squeal when braking is usually caused by the pads and rotors: worn pads touching their wear indicator, moisture or light rust, brake dust, or glazed friction surfaces.
A brief squeak during the first few stops in damp weather that then goes away is usually moisture or surface rust.
A squeal that is persistent, getting louder, or present on most stops suggests worn pads or another fault and should be inspected soon.
Grinding or a metal-on-metal scraping sound usually means the friction material is gone or something is caught in the brake, and can quickly damage the rotors.

brake light on after releasing handbrake
what does the abs light mean
brake system message on the dashboard

The ABS light means the anti-lock system has a fault. Normal braking usually still works, but the wheels can lock under hard braking. A red brake warning is more serious and can mean low brake fluid or a hydraulic problem.
Brake or ABS warning lamp, fluid loss, changed pedal feel, or reduced braking.

low or incorrect transmission fluid cause shifting problems
what is the correct transmission fluid capacity for my vehicle
Transmission slipping is when the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up as it should, or gears engage late or harshly.
Engine speed rises without expected acceleration, delayed engagement, harsh shifts, warning messages, or unusual noise.
Clutch, driveshaft, differential, and acceleration vibration
why does my car shake when I accelerate
Vibration when accelerating, or a slipping or juddering clutch, usually comes from the clutch, driveshafts, CV joints, engine mounts or differential.
Shudder or vibration during acceleration, a change with vehicle speed, noise, or engine-speed flare.
Tire pressure, tread, rotation, and replacement
how much air in my tires
how much air should i put

Check the pressures at least once a month with the tires cold (before driving, or after a few minutes parked), using the figures on the sticker in the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual for your exact car. Front and rear can differ, and many cars list a higher figure for a full load. Don't use the maximum printed on the tire: that's the tire's limit, not the car's setting.
Pressure warning, visible damage, low pressure, uneven wear, vibration, or reduced wet-road grip.
Steering, alignment, suspension, and wheel-bearing symptoms
Steering and suspension problems show up as clunks over bumps, a wandering or loose feel, uneven tire wear, a humming wheel bearing or the car pulling.
Pulling, wandering, excessive bounce, clunks, vibration, uneven tire wear, or humming that changes with speed.

one click and will not crank
loose ground causes intermittent electrical problems
what does a starter motor do
what does a car battery do
A car that won't start or cranks slowly usually has a weak battery, a poor battery connection, or a starter or charging problem.
Slow cranking, clicking, dimming lights, a battery warning light, needing jump-starts again and again, or stalling.
Dashboard warning lights and OBD diagnostic trouble codes
P0300 code does not prove spark plugs are bad
does diagnostic code P0300 prove the spark plugs are bad
Warning lights mean a system needs attention. Red lights (oil pressure, temperature, brakes, charging) usually mean stop soon; amber lights such as the check-engine light mean get it checked soon.
Warning lamp, stored or pending code, drivability change, or emissions-related notice.
Coolant, brake, transmission, and other fluid leaks
coolant color does not prove compatibility
Fluid under the car can be coolant, engine oil, brake fluid, transmission or power-steering fluid, or just water from the air-conditioning.
A puddle, a fluid level that keeps dropping, a smell, a warning light, overheating, or brakes, steering or gears behaving differently.
Filters, spark plugs, and routine preventive service
clogged fuel filter causes poor performance
do all cars have the same spark plug replacement interval
what does an air filter do
Air, cabin and fuel filters, spark plugs and other wear items are replaced at intervals set by the vehicle maker, by distance or time.
Reduced airflow, odor, rough running, or a service reminder may prompt inspection but do not determine a universal interval.
what maintenance is overdue at 60000 kilometers
calculate next service date without maintenance history
Maintenance schedules are based on both distance and time, whichever comes first. If a service is overdue, book it soon and check whether safety items such as brakes or tires were due.
A service reminder or a missing record is a reason to check the paperwork, not proof that a part has failed.
Before and after each rental, walk around the car and record its condition: body damage, tires, lights, warning lights, fuel level and mileage.
New damage, warning indicators, abnormal noises, fluid leaks, tire concerns, or customer-reported symptoms.

Inspect the safety items first: tires, brakes, steering, lights and any warning lights, then anything the service history shows is due. A vehicle-health assessment is only as good as its data and can't confirm a part's condition on its own.
A symptom should be recorded with when it occurs, warning indicators, and any inspection or scan results.
Interpreting maintenance model recommendations and scores
low model score prove vehicle is safe
The maintenance model's score shows how closely a vehicle's data resembles past cases that needed service. It's a prompt to inspect, not a confirmed fault.
A flagged category means the model's score passed its recommendation threshold; a low score doesn't prove the car has no faults.
Fleet maintenance prioritization and recurring issues
Prioritise fleet maintenance by safety first (brakes, tires, steering, warning lights), then overdue services, then recurring problems.
Repeated work orders, safety findings, overdue service and model recommendations are different kinds of evidence; report them separately.
Difference between a symptom, diagnostic code, and confirmed fault
difference between symptom DTC and diagnosis
confirm cause before replacing a part
A symptom is what you notice, a diagnostic trouble code shows which test or circuit failed, and a confirmed fault is what an inspection proves. A code alone doesn't tell you which part to replace.
A noise, warning light, vibration, smell or change in performance is something to note down, not proof that a particular part has failed.
Hybrid and electric vehicle high-voltage safety
do hybrids and electric cars use only one coolant circuit
Hybrid and electric cars use high-voltage systems that can cause a fatal electric shock. Never open, touch or cut the orange high-voltage cables or the battery pack.
A high-voltage or hybrid-system warning, reduced propulsion, charging interruption, unusual heat, smoke, odor, crash damage, or fluid intrusion warrants cautious handling.
Cabin heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning concerns
hybrid heater and defroster stopped working
Weak or warm air from the A/C usually comes from low refrigerant, a compressor problem, a blocked cabin filter or condenser, or a blower or control fault.
Compare airflow strength at available fan settings, vent temperature, selected mode, outside conditions, and whether the concern affects heating, cooling, or both.
Exhaust leaks, emissions controls, and diesel particulate filters
what does a catalytic converter do
Exhaust leaks, emission-control faults and a blocked diesel particulate filter (DPF) can cause loud exhaust noise, fumes, warning lights or reduced power.
Exhaust odor, ticking or hissing, smoke, reduced power, warning messages, or a scan code can help guide inspection but do not confirm a failed catalyst, sensor, EGR valve, or filter.
White smoke or steam from the exhaust

Thin white vapour that clears once the engine warms up is usually just condensation. Thick white smoke that keeps coming, especially with a sweet smell, can mean coolant is burning in the engine; a failed head gasket is one possible cause.

Warning signs that point toward a coolant problem: the coolant level keeps dropping with no visible leak, the engine overheats or the temperature gauge climbs, a sweet smell from the exhaust, bubbles in the coolant reservoir, a milky or creamy residue in the oil, or misfiring after a cold start.
Motorcycle chain, belt, and shaft final-drive concerns
Motorcycle chains, belts and shafts need regular inspection, cleaning, lubrication and tension adjustment as the owner's manual specifies.
Clicking, tight spots during wheel rotation, snatch or lash, visible damage, unusual slack, or a change after wheel service warrants inspection.
Grinding or scraping noise when braking
A grinding or metal-on-metal noise when braking usually means the pads are worn through and metal is rubbing the rotor, or something is caught in the brake.
Grinding that gets worse with harder braking, a vibrating pedal, the car pulling to one side when braking, or longer stopping distances.
Car shakes, shudders or vibrates when braking
Shaking or a pulsing pedal when braking usually means the brake rotors are uneven (often called warped), or there's a problem with the wheels, tires or suspension.

A steering wheel that shakes when braking points more to the front brakes; a pulsing pedal or seat shake can involve the rear. Shaking that continues without braking points to wheels, tires or suspension.
Car pulls or drifts to one side
A car that pulls or drifts to one side usually has uneven tire pressure, wheel misalignment, a dragging brake or a worn steering or suspension part.
Note whether it pulls all the time, only when braking, or only on some roads, and whether the steering wheel is off-centre when driving straight.
A flashing (blinking) check-engine light usually means a severe misfire that can quickly overheat and damage the catalytic converter.
Shaking or rough running, loss of power, a fuel or sulphur smell, or a hot exhaust can accompany it.
Blue or blue-grey smoke from the exhaust
Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke means the engine is burning oil.
The oil level drops between changes, oily deposits at the tailpipe, fouled spark plugs, or a burning-oil smell.
Black or dark sooty exhaust smoke means the engine is burning too much fuel for the air it gets: a rich mixture.
Higher fuel use, a fuel smell, soot at the tailpipe, reduced power, or a check-engine light.
Steering wheel shakes or vibrates at high speed
steering wheel shakes at high speed
A steering wheel that shakes at higher speeds is most often caused by unbalanced wheels, and sometimes by a damaged tire, a bent wheel or worn steering parts.
Shaking that starts at a certain speed and eases above or below it points to balance; shaking only when braking points to the brakes instead.
Clicking or popping noise when turning
clicking when turning the steering wheel
A clicking or popping noise when turning is most often a worn outer CV joint on a front-wheel-drive car, usually after its rubber boot has torn.
Clicking that gets faster with speed in a tight turn; grease splattered around the inside of the wheel; vibration when accelerating can point to an inner CV joint.
Battery or charging warning light while driving
battery light is on while driving
lights dim and the car stalled
A battery or charging light while driving means the charging system has a fault, usually an alternator that isn't charging, so the car is running on battery power and may stop.
Dimming lights, electrical items working poorly, a whining or squealing belt noise, and on some engines a rising temperature if the same belt drives the water pump.
Fluid leaking under the car: what the colour can suggest
water dripping from under the car
water under the car after using ac

The colour of a leak is a useful clue: clear water is usually A/C condensation, green, orange or pink can be coolant, brown or black is often engine oil, red can be transmission or power-steering fluid, and a clear-to-yellowish slippery fluid near a wheel can be brake fluid, and blue is usually windscreen-washer fluid.
A puddle or spots under the parked car, a falling fluid level, warning lights, overheating, or a change in how the brakes or steering feel.
If your tire is flat, slow down gradually and pull over somewhere safe, away from traffic. Turn on your hazard lights and don't keep driving on the flat tire.
The car pulling to one side, a flapping or thumping noise, heavy steering, or a tire-pressure warning light.
Steering is heavy or hard to turn
steering wheel is hard to turn
hard to turn the steering wheel
Steering that suddenly becomes heavy usually means power-steering assistance has been reduced or lost, or a front tire is low.
Note whether the steering became heavy suddenly or gradually, whether it is worse at low speed, and any whining noise or warning light.
Spongy, soft or sinking brake pedal
brake pedal goes to the floor
A spongy or soft brake pedal usually means air in the brake lines, low brake fluid from a leak, or a failing master cylinder. It reduces braking power.
The pedal travels further than normal, feels soft, or sinks while held down.

If your brakes fail while driving, pump the brake pedal firmly, shift to a lower gear, and apply the parking brake gradually while steering to a safe place. Turn on your hazard lights and use the horn to warn others.
The pedal goes to the floor or the car barely slows when braking.
Burning smell or electrical burning smell
A burning plastic or electrical smell can mean overheating wiring or a short circuit, which can start a fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.
A smell of hot plastic, rubber or wiring, sometimes with smoke, flickering lights or a blown fuse.
Smoke from under the hood or engine compartment
Smoke from under the bonnet can be steam from overheating coolant, oil burning on hot parts, or an electrical fire. Pull over safely, switch off the engine and get everyone out of the car.
Smoke or steam from the bonnet area, often with a smell or a temperature warning.
smell of gas in the car
A strong fuel smell or a fuel leak is a fire risk. Don't start or keep running the engine, keep away from ignition sources such as sparks, flames and cigarettes, and move away from the car.
A smell of petrol or diesel inside or around the car, or fuel dripping underneath.
If a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly and keep the car straight. Don't brake hard: ease off the accelerator, let the car slow down gradually, then steer to a safe place and stop.
A loud bang, then flapping noise, pulling to one side and vibration.
If you lose steering control while driving, stay calm, hold the wheel, turn on the hazard lights, ease off the accelerator and brake gently and steadily to stop. Don't brake hard or swerve.
The wheel won't turn, turns without the car responding, or becomes extremely heavy.
Sudden, severe shaking can mean a tire is failing, a wheel is loose, or there's a serious engine or drivetrain fault. Slow down gradually and stop somewhere safe.
Shaking through the whole car, steering wheel or seat that appears suddenly.
engine cranks but does not start
engine turns over but won't start
umaandar ang starter pero ayaw mag start
If the engine cranks normally but won't start, it usually isn't getting fuel, spark or enough air, or the immobiliser is blocking it.
The starter turns the engine at normal speed but it never fires.
Blown fuses and single electrical items not working
When one electrical item stops working, such as a light, the radio, a power outlet or a window, a blown fuse is a common cause.
One circuit stops working while the rest of the car is normal.
how long does a car battery last
how many years does a car battery last

Keep the battery terminals clean and tight and avoid leaving lights or accessories on with the engine off. Most car batteries last about 2 to 4 years in a hot climate, so have it tested once it's around 3 years old or if starting becomes slower.
Slower cranking, dim lights at start-up, or needing jump-starts.
Checking and topping up engine oil

Check the oil with the car on level ground and the engine off, as the owner's manual describes: wait a few minutes, pull out the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in, then pull it out again and read the level between the marks.
Oil level near or below the minimum mark.
Knocking, ticking or rattling engine noises
Engine noises point to different problems depending on the sound: knocking or pinging when accelerating, ticking from the top of the engine, rattling at start-up, or squealing from a belt.
A new noise that follows engine speed.
Transmission fluid lubricates, cools and operates the gearbox. Check and change it only as the owner's manual specifies; many modern automatics have no dipstick and need a workshop procedure.
Slipping, harsh shifts or a burning smell can follow low or worn fluid.
Hard to shift gears or grinding gears (manual)
Difficulty selecting gears in a manual car usually comes from a clutch that isn't fully disengaging, low clutch fluid, worn synchronisers or a linkage problem.
Grinding, a gear lever that won't move, or gears that pop out.
Whining, humming or clunking from the transmission
Whining, humming or clunking from the transmission can come from low fluid, worn bearings or gears, worn mounts or driveline parts.
A noise that rises with speed or appears when changing gear.
Worn shock absorbers or struts make the car keep bouncing after bumps, dive when braking and lean more in corners, and they can lengthen stopping distances.
Bouncing, nose-dive under braking, knocking over bumps.
Wheel alignment sets the angles of the wheels. Signs it's off include pulling to one side, a crooked steering wheel when driving straight, and uneven tire wear.
Pulling, an off-centre steering wheel, uneven tire wear.
squealing when i turn the steering wheel all the way
noise when turning the wheel all the way
squealing when turning the steering wheel
whining when turning the steering wheel
A whining or groaning noise when turning the wheel on a car with hydraulic power steering often means low power-steering fluid or a worn pump.
Whining that rises when turning, sometimes with heavier steering.

Uneven wear has typical patterns: both edges worn usually means under-inflation, the centre worn means over-inflation, one edge worn usually means misalignment, and patchy or cupped wear points to suspension or balance problems.
Wear concentrated on edges, the centre, one side or in patches.
Wheel balancing evens out the weight around each wheel and tire so they spin smoothly. Unbalanced wheels usually cause vibration through the steering wheel at certain speeds.
Steering-wheel vibration in a speed range, scalloped wear.

Rotate the tires about every 8,000 to 10,000 km, conveniently at every second oil change, so they wear evenly and last longer. Follow the pattern in the owner's manual: some tires and cars need a specific one.
Front and rear tires wearing at different rates.
Tire sidewall bulge, bubble or cut
A bulge, bubble or deep cut in the sidewall means the tire's internal structure is damaged and it can burst. Don't drive on it: stop safely and fit the spare or call roadside assistance.
A visible bulge or bubble on the side of the tire, or a cut showing cords.

Coolant protects the engine from overheating, freezing and corrosion. Check the level in the reservoir with the engine cold, and replace it at the interval in the owner's manual using the specified coolant type.
Coolant below the minimum mark, or needing frequent top-ups.

Brake fluid transmits the pedal pressure to the brakes. It absorbs moisture over time, so it's replaced at the interval in the owner's manual. A slowly dropping level can be pad wear; a fast drop means a leak.
Level below the minimum mark, a brake warning light.
Reporting damage to a rental vehicle
what if i damage the car
If a rental car is damaged, take clear photos, note when and where it happened, and report it to the rental team as soon as possible, before arranging any repairs.
Scratches, dents, broken glass or lights found during or after a rental.
Reporting a fault with a rental vehicle
report a problem with the car

If something seems wrong with a rental car, tell the rental team straight away: what you noticed, when it started, any warning lights and the mileage. Don't arrange repairs yourself unless they ask you to.
Any warning light, noise, smell or change in how the car drives.
What OBD-II code letters and numbers mean
what does the first letter of a code mean
difference between p0 and p1 codes

OBD-II codes have five characters. The letter shows the system: P for powertrain, B for body, C for chassis and U for network. P0 and P2 codes are generic, P1 codes are manufacturer-specific, and P3 codes are split between generic and manufacturer-specific.
A code such as P0301 or P1456 from a scan tool.
Musty or mouldy smell from the air-conditioning
A musty or mouldy smell from the vents usually comes from moisture and mould on the A/C evaporator, or a dirty cabin air filter.
Musty or mouldy smell from the air-conditioning.
Brake pedal is hard to press
have to press brake very hard
A brake pedal that's hard to press usually means the brake booster isn't assisting, often because of a vacuum leak or a failed booster. The brakes still work, but they need much more force.
Brake pedal is hard to press.
can i put water in my radiator
Plain water can be used briefly in an emergency to get the car to a workshop, but it doesn't protect the engine against corrosion, freezing or boiling the way coolant does.
If your car is on fire, stop as soon as it's safe, switch off the engine, get everyone out and move well away from the car, then call emergency services.
Swollen, leaking, hot or hissing battery
A swollen, leaking, very hot or hissing battery is a hazard: it can release flammable gas and corrosive acid. Don't touch it, switch off the engine, and keep sparks and flames away.
Swollen, leaking, hot or hissing battery.
A rotten-egg (sulfur) smell usually comes from the catalytic converter, often because the engine is running rich, or from an overcharged battery releasing gas.
what does the tpms light mean
tire light still on after adding air
The TPMS light means one or more tires is well below its correct pressure. On many cars, a light that flashes for about a minute and then stays on means the monitoring system itself has a fault.
Key fob or remote not working
A key fob that stops working usually has a flat battery. Most cars also give you a way to start or unlock the car with a weak fob; the owner's manual describes it.
Key fob or remote not working.
Wrong fuel put in the tank
If you've put the wrong fuel in, don't start the engine. If you're already driving, stop as soon as it's safe and switch off.
Wrong fuel put in the tank.
Jump-starting a car with a flat battery
how to jump start a car

To jump-start a car you need jumper cables and a working car or a jump pack. With both cars off, connect red to the flat battery's positive (+) terminal, then red to the good battery's positive, then black to the good battery's negative (-), and finally black to bare, unpainted metal on the dead car's engine, away from the battery.
manual or automatic which is better

A manual transmission has a clutch pedal and a gear lever, so you change gears yourself. A conventional automatic changes between a fixed set of gears for you. A CVT (continuously variable transmission) is also automatic, but it has no fixed gears: a belt or chain between two variable pulleys changes the ratio smoothly, so you feel no gear shifts.

Engine braking means slowing the car by lifting off the accelerator or selecting a lower gear, so the engine's resistance slows the wheels instead of the brakes alone. It's normal and safe, and on long downhill roads it keeps the brakes from overheating.
how to change a flat tire

Stop on firm, level ground away from traffic, turn on the hazard lights and apply the parking brake. Loosen the wheel nuts slightly while the wheel is on the ground, jack the car up at the point shown in the owner's manual, remove the nuts and wheel, and fit the spare. Lower the car, then tighten the nuts fully in a criss-cross pattern.
Car vibrates or shakes at idle
shakes when i start it in the morning
Shaking at idle usually means the engine is running unevenly, often from a misfire, or that worn engine mounts are letting normal engine vibration through to the cabin.
Vibration felt through the seat, steering wheel or floor while stopped with the engine running.
diesel or petrol which is better

A gasoline (petrol) engine ignites its fuel with a spark plug; a diesel engine has no spark plugs and ignites the fuel by compressing air until it is hot enough. Diesels usually use less fuel and pull harder at low engine speed, which suits heavy loads and long drives; gasoline engines are usually quieter, smoother and rev more freely.

Use the fuel grade (octane or RON number) given in the owner's manual or on the fuel-filler flap. If premium is only recommended, regular is usually fine with slightly less power; if premium is required, using regular can cause knocking and engine damage over time. A higher grade than the manual asks for brings no benefit.
The hazard lights are switched on and off with the button marked with a red triangle, usually in the middle of the dashboard. They flash all the turn signals at once to warn other drivers.
Dim headlights usually come from cloudy or yellowed lenses or ageing bulbs. If the lights also dim when the engine idles or other electrics act up, the battery or charging system may be weak.
Lights that look weak or yellow, or that dim when the engine idles.
Car uses more fuel than usual
A car that suddenly uses more fuel usually has a simple cause you can check first, such as low tire pressure, before an engine fault is likely.
Filling up more often than usual for the same driving.
how does a hybrid car work
engine turns off at stop hybrid

A hybrid combines a gasoline engine with an electric motor and battery. The car switches between them, or uses both, by itself: the engine often switches off when you stop or drive slowly, and the battery recharges while you brake. That's normal, and the READY light means the car is on even when it's silent.
how to charge an electric car
how do i charge an ev
how long to charge an electric car
how far can an electric car go
paano mag charge ng electric car

An electric car charges from a home or public charging point through the cable and connector type it was built for. Charging time depends on the charger: an ordinary outlet can take a whole night, while a public fast charger can add most of the range in under an hour. Range drops with highway speed, heavy loads and air conditioning.
Regenerative braking in hybrids and EVs
car slows when i lift off

Regenerative braking uses the electric motor to slow the car and turn that energy back into battery charge, so a hybrid or EV slows down noticeably when you lift off the accelerator. The normal brakes still work and take over for harder or slower stops.
Slipping clutch in a manual car
engine revs but car doesn't speed up manual
revs go up but car is slow
A slipping clutch lets the engine rev without the car speeding up as it should, usually in a high gear or going uphill. It's most often a worn clutch plate, and it gets worse over time.
Engine revs rising without matching speed, a burning smell, or the clutch biting very high.
A horn that stops working usually has a blown fuse or relay, a loose connection, or a faulty horn unit or steering-wheel contact.
No sound, or a weak sound, when pressing the horn.
may tubig sa loob ng sasakyan
Water inside the car usually comes from blocked sunroof or air-conditioning drains, or from worn door or window seals. A wet passenger floor after using the A/C often means a blocked A/C drain.
Damp carpets, a musty smell, or water dripping inside after rain or A/C use.
A burning smell has a few common sources, and the kind of smell tells them apart: burning rubber, burnt oil, hot brakes, melting plastic or a sweet syrupy smell.
Engine stalls or dies at idle

An engine that dies at idle usually has an idle that's too low or unstable: a dirty throttle body or idle control valve, an air leak, or a fuel delivery problem. A misfire or a failing sensor can do it too.
Engine stalls or dies at idle.
Car jerks, hesitates or loses power when accelerating
Jerking, hesitation or loss of power when you accelerate usually comes from the engine not getting enough spark, fuel or air, or from the transmission slipping.
Car jerks, hesitates or loses power when accelerating.
Accelerator not responding or reduced power (limp mode) with the engine light on

When the accelerator stops responding, or the car will barely speed up, and the check-engine light is on, the engine computer has usually found a fault in the electronic throttle system and switched to limp mode: it limits power and engine speed to protect the engine and keep the car controllable.
The accelerator pedal does little or nothing, or the car will not go above low speed, with the check-engine light on.
The engine stays at low revs or drops to idle when the pedal is pressed.
Car is hard to start or takes long to start
hard to start in the morning
slow to start in the morning
takes a few tries to start

A car that cranks a long time before starting usually has a weak battery, fuel pressure that drains away overnight, or (on a diesel) worn glow plugs. In the morning a cold engine needs more from all of them.
Car is hard to start or takes long to start.
Rattling noise from under the car

A rattle from under the car is most often a loose exhaust heat shield, a broken exhaust hanger or clamp, or loose parts inside the catalytic converter. If it happens over bumps instead, it's usually suspension: worn sway-bar links or bushings.
Rattling noise from under the car.
Windscreen wipers slow, streaking or not working
Slow or weak wipers usually mean a tired wiper motor, a stiff or worn linkage, or low voltage; streaks and squeaks mean the blades are worn or the glass is dirty.
Windscreen wipers slow, streaking or not working.
what color should engine oil be

Engine oil starts amber and darkens as it cleans the engine, so dark or black oil is normal after some driving, and diesel oil turns black almost straight away. What matters is the level and the change interval. Milky, coffee-coloured oil is not normal: it means coolant is getting into the oil, often a head-gasket problem.
Engine speed goes up and down at idle
rpm going up and down at idle

An idle that keeps rising and falling (hunting) usually means the engine is getting unmetered air from a vacuum leak, or the idle control can't hold a steady speed because the throttle body or idle valve is dirty.
Engine speed goes up and down at idle.
Engine feels weak or stalls with the A/C on
loses power when the ac is on

The A/C compressor takes some engine power, so a small engine feels a little weaker with it on; that's normal. A big drop in power, stalling or the engine shaking points to a tired engine (worn plugs, dirty throttle body), a slipping or tight A/C compressor, or an idle that isn't raised enough for the A/C load.
Engine feels weak or stalls with the A/C on.
Temperature gauge stays low or doesn't move
A temperature gauge that stays low usually means a thermostat stuck open (the engine never warms up, the heater blows cool and fuel use rises) or a faulty temperature sensor or gauge.
Temperature gauge stays low or doesn't move.

If all the windows stopped, check the fuse and the window lock button on the driver's door. If only one window stopped, its switch, regulator or motor is the usual cause; a grinding or clicking noise points to the regulator.
Car beeps when a door is opened
beeps when i open the door
chime when i open the door
nag beep pag binuksan ang pinto

A beep when you open the door is a reminder: the key is still in the ignition, the headlights are on, or the car is still in a gear other than Park. If it keeps beeping with all of those sorted, a door switch or seat-belt sensor may be faulty.
Car beeps when a door is opened.
Key won't turn in the ignition

When the key won't turn, the steering lock is usually holding the ignition. Turn the steering wheel gently left and right while you turn the key; it releases the lock. On an automatic, make sure the selector is fully in Park.
Key won't turn in the ignition.
Grinding or humming from a wheel
humming noise that gets louder with speed

A hum or growl that gets louder with speed, and changes when you turn one way, is the classic sign of a worn wheel bearing. A grinding noise when turning can also come from a stone in the brake shield or a worn CV joint.
Grinding or humming from a wheel.
What ABS (anti-lock braking) is and how it works
ABS stands for anti-lock braking system. In a hard stop it rapidly pulses the brakes on any wheel that is about to lock, so the tires keep grip and you can still steer while braking.
What ABS (anti-lock braking) is and how it works.

The airbag (SRS) light means the car has found a fault in the airbag system, so the airbags or seat-belt pretensioners may not work in a crash. It's normal for it to light briefly when you start the car and then go out.
The EPS light means the electric power-steering system has a fault. The car can still be steered, but the steering may suddenly feel much heavier, especially at low speed and when parking.
Signs of a weak or dying car battery
how do i know if my battery is dying
how do i know if my battery is weak
how to tell if battery is bad

The usual signs of a weak battery are slow or laboured cranking, especially in the morning, dim lights or a flickering dashboard when starting, clicking when you turn the key, and needing jump starts. A battery that is over about 3 years old in a hot climate is more likely to fail.
Slow cranking, especially when cold or in the morning.
Dim lights or a flickering dashboard when starting.
A swollen battery case or a rotten-egg smell.
Which engine oil type and grade to use

Use the oil grade (viscosity, such as 0W-20 or 5W-30) and the specification (such as API SP or ILSAC GF-6) listed in the owner's manual or on the oil filler cap. The grade matters more than the brand.
Which engine oil type and grade to use.
Periodic maintenance service (PMS) and how often to service a car
what is included in a pms
how often should i service my car
how often should my car be serviced
how often to service a car
what is included in a car service
what do they check during service

A PMS (periodic or preventive maintenance service) is the regular service in the owner's manual, usually every 5,000 to 10,000 km or every 6 months, whichever comes first. A typical PMS includes an oil and oil-filter change and checks of the brakes, tires, fluids, belts, battery, lights and filters.
Periodic maintenance service (PMS) and how often to service a car.
Car caught in a flood or driven through deep water
If the car has been in a flood, don't try to start it: water in the engine can bend internal parts the moment it turns over, and wet electrics can short. Have it towed and inspected first.
Car caught in a flood or driven through deep water.
How to save fuel and improve fuel economy
The biggest savings come from how you drive: accelerate and brake smoothly, keep a steady speed, and avoid long idling. Keeping the tires at the correct pressure and the car serviced also helps.
How to save fuel and improve fuel economy.
when should i replace my tires

Replace a tire when the tread is worn down to the wear bars (about 1.6 mm), when it has a bulge, a deep cut or cracks in the sidewall, or when it's more than about 5 to 6 years old even if the tread looks fine.

Predictive maintenance means servicing a part when its condition data says it's heading for failure, instead of on a fixed calendar or after it breaks. You measure or inspect the car regularly, watch the trend, and act when the trend crosses a limit.
Preventive vs predictive vs reactive maintenance
difference between preventive and predictive maintenance

Reactive maintenance fixes things after they break. Preventive maintenance services on a fixed schedule (every 5,000 or 10,000 km or every 6 months), whether the part needs it or not. Predictive (condition-based) maintenance services when inspections or data show the part is wearing out.
Preventive vs predictive vs reactive maintenance.

Condition-based maintenance acts on what an inspection finds. Each assessment rates every system (engine, brakes, tires and so on) and records measurements and warning lights; a rating that drops between assessments is the earliest warning you get.

A reassessment is the regular repeat inspection of a vehicle. In this system every vehicle is reassessed 30 days after its latest assessment; it shows as due soon within 7 days of that date and overdue after it.
Typical service life and intervals of car components
how long do car parts last
how long does a timing belt last
how long does a clutch last
how long does transmission fluid last
how often should brake pads be replaced
how often to replace brake pads
how often should tires be replaced
how often should i replace my battery
how often to replace timing belt

Typical ranges (the owner's manual decides for each car): engine oil 5,000 to 10,000 km; air filter 20,000 to 40,000 km; cabin filter 15,000 to 20,000 km; spark plugs 40,000 km (copper) to 100,000 km (iridium); brake pads 30,000 to 70,000 km; brake fluid every 2 years; coolant 2 to 5 years; automatic or CVT fluid 40,000 to 80,000 km; timing belt 60,000 to 100,000 km; battery 2 to 4 years; tires 40,000 to 80,000 km or 5 to 6 years; shock absorbers 80,000 to 100,000 km; clutch 80,000 to 150,000 km.
Typical service life and intervals of car components.
Early warning signs before a failure, by system
what to look for before breakdown
how to know a part will fail

Most failures give warning first. Engine: rough idle, hesitation, a check-engine light, oil use. Brakes: squeal, longer stops, a soft or pulsing pedal. Transmission: late or harsh shifts, slipping, dark or burnt fluid. Cooling: the gauge creeping up, coolant dropping, a sweet smell. Battery and charging: slow cranking, dim lights. Suspension and steering: clunks, wandering, uneven tire wear. Tires: tread under 3 mm, bulges, slow leaks.
Early warning signs before a failure, by system.

Fix in this order: safety first (brakes, tires, steering, anything rated critical), then anything that can cause a bigger failure if left (overheating, low oil pressure, a slipping transmission), then overdue scheduled service, then wear items trending down, then comfort items like the A/C.
The cost of downtime in a rental fleet
how much does a breakdown cost

In a rental fleet a breakdown costs far more than the repair: the lost rental days, the replacement car or refund for the customer, towing, rushed parts, and the customer you may not see again. A planned repair on a day with no booking costs only the repair.
The cost of downtime in a rental fleet.
when to replace a fleet vehicle

Rules of thumb: replace a car when a single repair would cost more than about half its resale value, when repair and downtime costs per kilometre keep rising while its value falls, or when the same safety system keeps failing. Many rental fleets rotate cars after about 3 to 5 years or 100,000 to 150,000 km, before major repairs start and while resale value is still good.

Track a few numbers per car and for the fleet: availability (days rentable out of days owned), breakdowns per 10,000 km, maintenance cost per km, scheduled-service compliance (services done on time), and repeat repairs (the same fault fixed twice within 90 days).
what data is needed for predictive maintenance

Predictions are only as good as the history behind them. For every car record: regular assessments with ratings and measurements, the odometer and date of every service, what was found and what was replaced, the cost, and the verified outcome of each recommendation (fault confirmed, repaired, or no fault found).
False alarms and missed faults in predictions
why does the model flag healthy cars

Every prediction trades two errors: a false alarm (inspecting a car that was fine) and a missed fault (a car that fails without warning). For safety systems a missed fault is the costly one, so models are tuned to catch most faults (high recall) and accept some false alarms; an inspection settles each alert.
False alarms and missed faults in predictions.

Most owner's manuals have a severe-service schedule with shorter intervals, for stop-and-go traffic, short trips, heat, dust, heavy loads or flooded roads. Rental cars in city traffic in the Philippines usually qualify, so plan by the severe schedule.
why does the same part keep failing

A part that fails again soon after repair usually means the cause wasn't fixed, only the symptom: a battery that keeps dying with a bad alternator or a drain, pads that wear fast because a caliper sticks, a radiator hose that keeps bursting because the cap or thermostat is bad.
what should a maintenance record include

A useful record has the date, the odometer, what was checked, what was found, what was replaced (part and brand), the cost, who did it, and the next due date or km. Without the odometer and cost, no schedule or cost comparison can be calculated.
Telematics and OBD data for predictive maintenance

An OBD-II reader or telematics unit reports fault codes, coolant temperature, battery voltage, engine load and mileage automatically. Trends in those readings (a battery voltage that drops week by week, a coolant temperature that runs higher) warn of failures before a driver notices anything.
Telematics and OBD data for predictive maintenance.
Spare parts to keep for a rental fleet

Keep the fast-moving parts for your most common models: oil and filters, brake pads, wiper blades, bulbs and fuses, a battery for the most common size, and a good spare tire per car. Order slow-moving parts (clutches, alternators) when an assessment shows them trending down.
Spare parts to keep for a rental fleet.

You need both. The PMS replaces fluids and filters on schedule because their wear can't be seen; the assessment finds wear and defects in parts that wear unevenly, like brakes, tires and suspension. An assessment never replaces an oil change.
how much brake pad is left

Measure pad thickness at each assessment. New pads are about 10 to 12 mm; plan replacement at 3 mm and don't go below 2 mm. From two measurements you get a wear rate: for example 1 mm per 4,000 km at 5 mm left means about 8,000 km before the 3 mm limit.

Measure tread depth at each assessment. New tires have about 8 mm; 1.6 mm is the legal-style minimum, but grip in the wet drops sharply below 3 mm, so plan replacement there. Two measurements give a wear rate and a replacement date.

A battery tester's health or CCA result is the best predictor: plan replacement below about 60 to 70% health. A resting voltage under about 12.4 V after a night parked, slow cranking, or an age over 3 years in a hot climate are the other warnings.
Fluid checks as an early warning

Fluids show trouble early: engine oil that's milky (coolant getting in) or smells of fuel; coolant that's rusty or oily; transmission fluid that's dark or smells burnt; brake fluid that's dark (it absorbs moisture). Check level and condition at every assessment.
Fluid checks as an early warning.

Between rentals, a five-minute check catches most problems early: walk-around for damage, tire condition and pressure, all lights, dashboard warning lights at start-up, fluid levels, and the odometer. Ask the returning customer if anything felt wrong.
how much to budget for maintenance

Budget per car from its own history: last year's maintenance cost per km times the km you expect, plus the big scheduled items coming due (timing belt, tires, brakes, battery) by their intervals. Costs rise with age and mileage, so older cars need a bigger share.

Service intervals are by distance and time, whichever comes first, because oil, fluids, rubber and batteries age even when the car sits. A car that sits for weeks still needs its time-based service, and its battery and tires checked.
Central locking or door locks not working

When the central locking stops working, one door or all of them won't lock or unlock with the remote or the button. One door on its own usually points to that door's lock actuator; all doors together point to the key fob, a fuse or the locking control unit.
Central locking or door locks not working.
locked my keys in the car
nalock ko ang susi sa loob
locked keys inside the rental car
locked the key in the car

If the keys are locked inside, don't force a door or break a window: that costs far more than the call-out. Use a spare key, or call roadside assistance or a locksmith; on a rental, call the rental team first, since they may hold a spare and forced entry counts as damage.
Push-button start won't start, or key not detected
car won't start with push button
ayaw mag start ang push start
key not detected and it won't start
smart key not detected won't start

With push-button start, a car that won't start or says the key is not detected usually can't sense the smart key, most often because its battery is weak. Most cars let you start by holding the key fob against the start button, which reads it without its battery.
Push-button start won't start, or key not detected.
gear lever won't come out of park

An automatic that won't shift out of Park is usually held by the shift lock, which only releases when it senses the brake pedal. A failed brake-light switch or a blown fuse is the commonest cause, and the same fault often stops the brake lights working.
Speedometer, fuel gauge or other gauge not working

A gauge that stops or reads wrong usually has lost its sensor signal rather than the instrument itself failing. A speedometer that drops to zero, often with the ABS or traction light on, points to a wheel-speed or vehicle-speed sensor; a fuel gauge that sticks points to the fuel-level sender in the tank. All gauges dying at once points to the cluster's fuse or connection.
Speedometer, fuel gauge or other gauge not working.
Reverse camera or parking sensors not working
parking sensors beep for no reason

Parking cameras and sensors fail most often because they are dirty, wet or blocked; they beep constantly or show a blurred or black picture. A sensor that stays silent or a camera that never shows a picture after cleaning points to a damaged unit, its wiring or a fuse.
Reverse camera or parking sensors not working.

Cruise control refuses to set or switches itself off when a system it depends on reports a fault: most often the brake-light switch, a wheel-speed sensor or the ABS and stability system. Adaptive cruise also switches off when its radar or camera behind the grille or windscreen is dirty or blocked.
Brake lights, turn signals, fog lights or one headlight not working

A turn signal that blinks much faster than normal almost always means a bulb on that side has failed. Brake lights that don't work at all point to the brake-light switch or its fuse, while one brake light, tail light, fog light or headlight out on its own is usually the bulb.
Brake lights, turn signals, fog lights or one headlight not working.
Windows fogging up or defogger not working

Windows fog up when moist cabin air meets cold glass. The quickest fix is the air conditioning with the vents on the windscreen and fresh air from outside (recirculation off): the A/C dries the air. A rear defogger that doesn't clear the back window usually has a broken heating line, a blown fuse or a failed relay.
Windows fogging up or defogger not working.
Turbocharger problems: loss of boost, whistling or smoke

A turbo problem usually shows as a sudden loss of power (often with the engine light and limp mode), a loud whistle or siren-like whine, or blue-grey smoke from oil getting past worn turbo seals. A split boost hose or a stuck control valve is more common than the turbo itself failing.
Turbocharger problems: loss of boost, whistling or smoke.
4WD and AWD: modes, warning light and binding
how to use four wheel drive

Part-time 4WD (common on pickups and SUVs) is for loose or slippery surfaces only: using it on dry pavement makes the drivetrain bind and hop on tight turns and can damage it. Use 2H normally, 4H on mud, gravel or sand at road speeds, and 4L only for slow, steep or deep going. A flashing 4WD light usually means the shift hasn't finished.
4WD and AWD: modes, warning light and binding.
Seat belt not retracting, latching or locking

A seat belt that won't retract or pull out is usually twisted, dirty or caught in the retractor; one that won't latch usually has something stuck in the buckle. A belt that won't latch or hold must be fixed before that seat is used.
Seat belt not retracting, latching or locking.
Driving in heavy rain and hydroplaning (aquaplaning)

In heavy rain, slow down, double the gap to the car ahead and turn on your headlights. If the car hydroplanes, the steering suddenly feels light because the tyres are riding on water: ease off the accelerator, hold the wheel straight and don't brake hard or jerk the steering until the tyres grip again.
Driving in heavy rain and hydroplaning (aquaplaning).
Early warning device and roadside emergency kit
what to keep in the car
what to do if the car breaks down on the road

Philippine traffic rules require an early warning device: a reflective triangle placed behind the car when it stops on the road. Keep it with a working spare tyre, jack and wrench, a flashlight, a basic first-aid kit and the roadside or rental contact number.
Early warning device and roadside emergency kit.
Car not used for weeks or months
car sitting for a long time
car parked for a long time
starting a car after long storage
car not driven for a month

A car left unused for weeks most often has a flat battery, tyres that lost pressure, brake discs with surface rust that grinds for the first stops, and sometimes damage from rats chewing wiring. Check these before driving off.
Car not used for weeks or months.

A small stone chip can usually be repaired cheaply if it is dealt with before it spreads; heat, cold air on hot glass and road bumps make chips grow into cracks. A crack in the driver's line of sight, or one longer than about a hand's width, normally needs a new windscreen.

Metro Manila's number coding (UVVRP) keeps cars off main roads on one weekday by the last digit of the plate: 1 and 2 on Monday, 3 and 4 on Tuesday, 5 and 6 on Wednesday, 7 and 8 on Thursday, and 9 and 0 on Friday. Hours, window exemptions and which roads and cities enforce it are set by the MMDA and local governments and change, so check the current rules before driving.

Philippine expressways collect tolls by RFID stickers, and there are two systems: Autosweep (SLEX, Skyway, STAR, TPLEX and NAIAX) and Easytrip (NLEX, SCTEX, CAVITEX and CALAX). The car needs the right sticker for the expressway, with enough load, before reaching the gate.
Vacuum (air) leak: hissing, high or rough idle
A vacuum leak lets unmeasured air into the engine through a cracked hose, loose connection or leaking gasket. It often causes a hissing sound, a high or uneven idle and a lean-mixture code.
Hissing with the engine running, rough or high idle, hesitation, check-engine light with lean codes such as P0171.
Drive (serpentine) belt squeal, wear or breakage

The drive (serpentine or fan) belt turns the alternator, and on many cars the water pump, power-steering pump and A/C compressor. A squeal, especially at start-up or when turning the wheel, usually means the belt is slipping because it is worn, loose or contaminated.
Squeal at cold start, when turning the steering or switching on the A/C; cracks or shiny glazing on the ribs; battery light or heavy steering if it slips badly.
Warming up the engine before driving
how long to idle the car

Modern fuel-injected engines don't need a long idle to warm up. Starting the engine, letting the oil circulate briefly and then driving gently until the temperature gauge reaches normal warms it faster and wastes less fuel.
Long idling wastes fuel and warms the engine more slowly than gentle driving.
Engine and transmission mounts hold the engine in place and absorb its vibration. Worn mounts let the engine move, causing a clunk when shifting or accelerating and stronger vibration at idle.
Clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse or when accelerating hard, vibration felt in the cabin at idle, the engine visibly rocking.

The head gasket seals the joint between the engine block and cylinder head. When it fails, coolant, oil and combustion gases can mix, causing overheating, white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke, coolant loss with no visible leak or milky oil.
Coolant disappearing without a visible leak, white exhaust smoke that smells sweet, bubbles in the coolant reservoir, milky residue under the oil cap, repeated overheating.
Engine lacks power under load, uphill or with passengers

An engine that feels weak only under heavy load (uphill, full of passengers, overtaking) often isn't getting enough fuel, air or spark at high demand, or the clutch or transmission is slipping so the power doesn't reach the wheels.
If the engine revs rise without more speed, suspect clutch or transmission slip; if the revs struggle to rise, suspect fuel, air, ignition or exhaust restriction.
Backfiring or popping from the exhaust or intake
A backfire is fuel burning outside the cylinders, in the exhaust or intake, with a pop or bang. It points to an incorrect air-fuel mixture, ignition problems or an exhaust leak.
Popping when lifting off the accelerator, bangs when starting, often with rough running or a check-engine light.
Engine keeps running after it is switched off
engine keeps running after turning off
engine runs on after switch off

An engine that keeps running or sputtering after the key is turned off ('dieseling' or run-on) is usually igniting fuel from hot carbon deposits or is getting fuel it shouldn't, and an ignition switch fault can keep it powered.
The engine sputters, shakes or keeps idling for seconds after switch-off.
A high idle is normal for a short time after a cold start. If it stays high when warm, the engine may be getting extra air or the idle control isn't working properly.
Idle stays high after warm-up, the car creeps forward strongly in Drive, sometimes with a lean code.
PCV valve and crankcase ventilation problems
oil in the air filter box
oil coming out of the dipstick

The PCV (positive crankcase ventilation) valve removes gases that escape past the pistons and sends them back into the intake. A blocked or stuck valve can raise crankcase pressure, push oil past seals and cause rough idle or oil consumption.
Oil leaks appearing at seals, oil in the air intake, whistling at idle, rough idle, higher oil use.

The fuel pump sends fuel from the tank to the engine at the pressure it needs. A weak pump starves the engine under load, causing hesitation, loss of power uphill, hard starting or stalling, and a dead pump stops the engine from starting.
Power loss at high speed or uphill, stalling when hot, long cranking, whining from the rear seat area, no humming from the tank when the key is switched on.

The fuel filter traps dirt before it reaches the injectors. A clogged filter restricts fuel flow, which shows up first when the engine needs the most fuel: accelerating hard, climbing or carrying a load.
Hesitation or loss of power under load, rough running, hard starting, stalling.

Fuel injectors spray a precise amount of fuel into the engine. A clogged injector makes a cylinder run lean and misfire; a leaking one causes a rich mixture, fuel smell, hard hot starts or black smoke.
Misfire or rough idle on one cylinder, hesitation, fuel smell, black smoke, higher fuel use, a cylinder-specific misfire code.

If the engine sputters and stops with the fuel gauge near empty, move to a safe place, switch on the hazard lights and add fuel. Diesel engines may need the fuel system primed or bled after running dry.
Sputtering, loss of power then stalling, with the gauge at or near empty.
The low-fuel light means the tank has reached its reserve. How far you can still go varies by car and driving, so refuel as soon as you can rather than relying on the reserve.
A yellow or orange fuel-pump symbol, sometimes with a chime or a range reading.
Loose fuel cap and EVAP system codes

The EVAP system stops fuel vapour escaping from the tank. A loose, damaged or missing fuel cap is the most common reason for an EVAP leak code (such as P0455, P0456 or P0442) and a check-engine light soon after refuelling.
Steady check-engine light with an EVAP code, sometimes a faint fuel smell; the car drives normally.
Water in diesel fuel and the fuel-water separator light
Diesel fuel filters collect water in a separator. A water-in-fuel warning light means water needs draining; water reaching the injection system can damage expensive parts.
A water-in-fuel warning light, rough running, power loss, hard starting.
Spark plug replacement and worn spark plugs
Spark plugs wear gradually; worn plugs make starting harder, cause misfires and hesitation and raise fuel use. Replacement intervals vary widely by plug type and engine, so follow the owner's manual.
Hard starting, rough idle, misfire under acceleration, higher fuel consumption.

An ignition coil makes the high voltage that fires a spark plug. A failing coil usually causes a misfire on one cylinder, felt as shaking or jerking under load, often with a flashing or steady check-engine light and a code such as P0301 to P0306.
Rough idle, jerking when accelerating, misfire code for one cylinder, sometimes a fuel smell.
P0300 means random or multiple-cylinder misfires; P0301 to P0308 mean a misfire was detected in that cylinder number. They point to where to look, not which part failed.
Rough running, shaking, loss of power and a steady or flashing check-engine light.
Crankshaft or camshaft position sensor faults
car dies when hot no restart

The crankshaft and camshaft position sensors tell the engine computer where the engine is in its cycle. A failing sensor can make the engine stall suddenly, especially when hot, or crank without starting.
Sudden stalling, cranks but won't start (sometimes restarts after cooling down), a tachometer that drops to zero, codes such as P0335 or P0340.
P0420 and P0430: catalytic converter efficiency below threshold

P0420 (bank 1) and P0430 (bank 2) mean the oxygen sensors show the catalytic converter isn't cleaning the exhaust as well as it should. The converter may be worn, but a faulty oxygen sensor, an exhaust leak or an engine running rich or misfiring can also trigger it.
A steady check-engine light, usually with no change in how the car drives; sometimes a rotten-egg smell or failed emissions test.
Lean mixture codes P0171 and P0174

P0171 (bank 1) and P0174 (bank 2) mean the engine is getting too much air or too little fuel, and the computer has reached the limit of what it can correct. Both codes together usually point to a common cause.
Rough or high idle, hesitation, misfires, a steady check-engine light.
Rich mixture codes P0172 and P0175
P0172 (bank 1) and P0175 (bank 2) mean the engine is getting too much fuel or too little air. Running rich wastes fuel, fouls spark plugs and can damage the catalytic converter.
Black smoke, fuel smell, poor fuel economy, sooty spark plugs, rough idle.
P0128: engine takes too long to warm up (thermostat)
coolant temperature below thermostat regulating temperature
P0128 means the engine took longer than expected to reach its normal operating temperature, most often because the thermostat is stuck open. A faulty coolant temperature sensor can also cause it.
The temperature gauge stays low or rises slowly, weak cabin heat, higher fuel use, a steady check-engine light.

Oxygen sensors measure oxygen in the exhaust so the engine computer can adjust the fuel mixture and monitor the catalytic converter. A failing sensor can raise fuel use and trigger a check-engine light; heater-circuit codes such as P0135 or P0141 are common.
Steady check-engine light, higher fuel consumption, rough idle, failed emissions test.

The mass airflow (MAF) sensor measures the air entering the engine. A dirty or faulty sensor misreads airflow, which can cause hesitation, stalling, rough idle, poor fuel economy and lean or rich codes.
Hesitation, stalling after starting, rough idle, poor economy, codes such as P0101 or P0171.

The EGR (exhaust gas recirculation) valve sends a small amount of exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperatures and emissions. A clogged or stuck valve can cause rough idle, stalling, pinging or a check-engine light with codes such as P0401.
Rough idle or stalling (valve stuck open), knocking or pinging under load (stuck closed), black smoke or power loss in diesels.

The throttle body controls how much air enters the engine. Carbon build-up can cause a rough or unstable idle and stalling; an electronic throttle fault can cause poor response and reduced-power mode.
Unstable or low idle, stalling when stopping, delayed throttle response, reduced-power warning.
P0700 means the transmission computer has stored its own fault code. It doesn't say what is wrong by itself; the transmission module's codes must be read with a suitable scanner.
Harsh or delayed shifts, stuck in one gear (limp mode), a check-engine or transmission light.
U-codes (U0100 and similar) mean one control module stopped receiving messages from another over the vehicle network. Causes range from a weak battery to wiring faults or a failed module.
Several warning lights at once, gauges dropping out, starting problems, the car in reduced-power mode.
P0500 means the engine computer isn't getting a valid vehicle-speed signal. The speedometer may stop working, shifting can become erratic and ABS or traction lights may come on.
Speedometer dead or jumping, harsh or odd shifting, cruise control not working, ABS light.
Clearing trouble codes or resetting the check-engine light

Clearing codes only turns off the light; it doesn't fix the fault, and the light returns if the problem remains. Clearing also erases information a mechanic could use and makes the car show 'not ready' for an emissions test.
The light returning after being cleared means the fault is still present.
Reading trouble codes with an OBD-II scanner

Cars sold in most markets since the late 1990s or 2000s have an OBD-II port, usually under the dashboard near the steering wheel. A code reader shows stored trouble codes, which point to the system that detected a fault rather than the exact failed part.
A code describes what the computer detected; the cause still needs to be tested.

The thermostat controls coolant flow to the radiator. Stuck closed, it makes the engine overheat quickly, often with the radiator hose staying cool; stuck open, the engine warms slowly, the heater is weak and fuel use rises.
Stuck closed: fast overheating, upper radiator hose cool while the engine is hot. Stuck open: gauge stays low, weak heater, code P0128.

The water pump circulates coolant through the engine and radiator. A failing pump often leaks coolant from its weep hole, makes a grinding or whining noise, or stops circulating coolant, causing overheating.
Coolant drips or crusty residue near the front of the engine, whining or grinding that changes with revs, rising temperature.

The radiator fan pulls air through the radiator when the car is slow or stopped. If it doesn't work, the engine usually stays cool on the highway but overheats in traffic or at idle, and the A/C may also blow warm when stopped.
Temperature rises in traffic and drops when driving faster, the fan doesn't run when the engine is hot or the A/C is switched on.
The radiator or coolant cap keeps the cooling system under pressure, which raises the coolant's boiling point. A worn cap seal lets coolant escape as steam, causing slow coolant loss and overheating.
Coolant loss with no visible leak, coolant pushed into or out of the reservoir, steam near the cap, overheating.
Heater core leak: sweet smell and foggy windows inside

The heater core is a small radiator behind the dashboard that heats the cabin. When it leaks, coolant vapour causes a sweet smell inside, a greasy fog on the windscreen and sometimes a wet floor on the passenger side.
Sweet smell in the cabin, oily fog on the inside of the windscreen, damp carpet, slowly falling coolant level.
A red thermometer symbol means the engine is overheating; a blue one (on some cars) means the engine is still cold. A red temperature light needs immediate action to avoid serious engine damage.
Red thermometer symbol, gauge in the red, steam from the hood, a sweet coolant smell.
A radiator blocked inside by deposits or outside by dirt, insects or bent fins can't shed enough heat, so the engine runs hot, especially in traffic, uphill or with the A/C on.
Gradually rising temperature under load, cold spots on the radiator, visible debris or green crusty leaks.

A CVT (continuously variable transmission) uses a belt or chain between variable pulleys instead of fixed gears. Common complaints are a whining noise, shuddering when pulling away, a rubber-band feel or the car going into reduced-power mode when the CVT overheats.
Whining that rises with speed, shudder from a stop, delayed take-off, engine revs flaring without matching acceleration, a transmission warning light.
Transmission overheating or transmission temperature warning

A transmission temperature warning means the fluid is too hot, usually from heavy loads, steep climbs, towing, slow traffic in hot weather or low fluid. Hot fluid breaks down quickly and can damage the transmission.
A transmission temperature light or message, burnt smell, slipping or harsh shifts.
Harsh, jerky or delayed automatic shifts

Harsh or jerky automatic shifts usually mean the transmission's fluid, control or engine mounts need attention. Many transmissions also adapt their shifts, so a recent battery disconnection can make shifts feel firm for a while.
Bang or jolt on a particular gear change, delayed shifts, flare of revs between gears, warning light.
Clutch pedal sticks, sinks or feels soft

A clutch pedal that sinks, stays down or feels soft usually means a problem in the clutch hydraulic system (master or slave cylinder or fluid) or the clutch cable, so the clutch can't fully disengage and gears become hard to select.
Pedal sinks or stays near the floor, gears grind or won't engage, fluid leak near the pedal or gearbox.
Noise when pressing or releasing the clutch

A noise that appears or disappears when you press the clutch pedal points to the clutch area: a whirring or chirping with the pedal pressed often means a worn release bearing; a noise with the pedal released and in neutral can come from the gearbox input bearing.
Whirring, chirping or grinding that changes with clutch pedal position.

The differential lets the drive wheels turn at different speeds. A whine that changes when accelerating or lifting off, or a rumble from the axle, can mean low differential oil or worn gears or bearings.
Whine or howl that changes with acceleration or coasting, oil leaking at the axle or differential housing.
Manual gearbox jumps out of gear
A manual gearbox that jumps out of gear, often on acceleration or deceleration, usually has worn internal parts, worn gearbox mounts or a linkage problem.
The lever moves back to neutral by itself in a particular gear.
Engine runs but car won't move in gear
engine runs but car doesn't move

If the engine runs but the car doesn't move in gear, drive isn't reaching the wheels: very low transmission fluid, a failed clutch, a broken axle or driveshaft, or a stuck parking brake are common causes.
Engine revs but no movement, clunk or grinding when selecting gear, fluid under the car.
Parking brake (handbrake) sticking or not holding

A parking brake that sticks, drags or doesn't hold usually has a seized cable or caliper, worn rear brakes or, on electronic parking brakes, a motor or switch fault. A dragging brake makes a wheel hot and can smell of burning.
Lever or switch released but the car feels held back, one rear wheel hot or smelling, the car rolls on a slope with the brake on, a parking brake warning light.
A sticking caliper keeps a pad pressed on the disc. The car may pull to one side, feel sluggish, smell of hot brakes, and one wheel gets much hotter than the others.
Pulling to one side when braking or driving, burning smell, one hot wheel, uneven pad wear.
Traction control or stability control (ESC) light

A flashing traction or stability control light (a car with wavy lines) means the system is working to stop wheel spin or a skid, so ease off the accelerator. A light that stays on means the system is off or has a fault and won't help in a skid.
Flashing on slippery roads or hard acceleration (normal); constantly on, often with the ABS or check-engine light (fault).
Brake lights stuck on or not working

The brake light switch at the brake pedal turns the brake lights on. A faulty switch can leave the lights on all the time (draining the battery) or off; on many cars it also affects cruise control, the shift lock and starting.
Brake lights on when the pedal isn't pressed, or not on when it is; shifter won't leave Park; cruise control not working.

Brake discs wear and can develop uneven thickness that causes pulsation through the pedal or steering. Whether they can be resurfaced depends on their remaining thickness against the minimum marked on the disc or in the service information.
Pulsing brake pedal or steering-wheel shake when braking, deep grooves, a lip at the disc edge.

Ball joints connect the wheels to the suspension arms and let them steer and move. Worn joints cause clunking over bumps, wandering steering and uneven tire wear; a joint that separates can make a wheel collapse.
Clunk or knock over bumps or when turning, loose or wandering steering, uneven inner or outer tire wear.
Worn tie-rod ends and loose steering
Tie-rod ends link the steering rack to the wheels. When they or the rack wear, the steering feels loose with free play before the car responds, the car wanders and the tires wear unevenly.
Free play at the steering wheel, wandering on straight roads, knocking when turning over bumps, feathered tire wear.
Sway bar (stabiliser) links connect the anti-roll bar to the suspension. Worn links are a very common cause of a knock or clunk over bumps and rough roads, especially at low speed.
Knocking or rattling over uneven roads and speed bumps, more body roll in corners.
Car sagging or sitting low on one corner
A car that sits lower at one corner or at the back usually has a weak or broken coil spring, or a failed air or leaf spring. It changes handling, braking and headlight aim and can let the tire rub.
One corner visibly lower, clunk when turning or over bumps, tire rubbing, the car leaning.
Power-steering fluid leak or low fluid

Hydraulic power steering uses fluid pressurised by a pump. A leak lowers the level, causing whining when turning, heavier steering and eventually pump damage. Cars with electric power steering have no fluid.
Whine when turning, heavy steering at low speed, red or clear oily drips near the front, falling reservoir level.

A wobble felt at low speed, rather than a vibration at high speed, often comes from a bent wheel, a damaged tire with a shifted belt, or loose wheel nuts. Loose wheel nuts are dangerous: the wheel can come off.
Wobble or side-to-side movement at walking or low speed, thumping, a visible wobble when the wheel turns.
Squeaks and creaks over bumps or when turning usually come from dry or worn rubber bushings, ball joints, strut top mounts or sway-bar bushings.
Squeak or creak at low speed over bumps, when turning at parking speed or when the car rocks.
Tire noise and humming on the road

Tire noise that changes with road surface is normal, but a growing hum, drone or rhythmic noise can mean uneven (cupped or feathered) wear, low pressure, or a worn wheel bearing, which sounds similar.
Hum or roar that rises with speed; uneven or scalloped tread; a noise that changes when steering left or right suggests a bearing.

Tires age even when the tread looks fine: the rubber hardens and cracks, which reduces grip and raises the risk of failure. The manufacture date is in the DOT code on the sidewall; tire and vehicle makers give guidance on maximum age.
Fine cracks in the sidewall or between tread blocks, hard rubber, a spare tire that has never been used but is old.
A tire that needs air every few days usually has a small puncture, a leaking valve or valve core, or a poor seal between tire and rim from corrosion or a bent rim.
Pressure drops every few days, TPMS light returns, one tire looks lower.

Nitrogen loses pressure slightly more slowly than air, but normal air (which is mostly nitrogen) works fine. What matters most is checking and keeping the correct pressure; you can top up a nitrogen-filled tire with air.
Driving on a temporary (space-saver) spare tire

A temporary space-saver spare is for getting to a tire shop, not for everyday driving. It has its own speed and distance limits, printed on the tire or in the owner's manual, and the car may brake and handle differently.
A narrower spare with a label showing its maximum speed and pressure.
Wheel nuts after a tire change

Wheel nuts must be tightened to the correct torque in a cross pattern. After changing a wheel or having tire work done, it is good practice to recheck them after a short distance, because loose nuts can let the wheel come off.
Clicking or wobble from a wheel, vibration that started after tire work.

The alternator charges the battery and powers the electrics while the engine runs. When it fails, the battery light usually comes on and the car runs on battery power until it goes flat, so lights dim, electrics act strangely and the engine eventually stalls.
Battery light while driving, dim or flickering lights, whining from the engine, a battery that keeps going flat.
Battery drains when the car is parked (parasitic drain)

A battery that goes flat after sitting for a day or two is either weak or something keeps drawing current with the car off: a light left on, a glovebox or boot light, an aftermarket accessory, a module that doesn't go to sleep, or a stuck relay.
Flat battery after the car is parked, especially after a few days; a battery that tests good when charged.

The starter motor cranks the engine. A single click with no cranking, a grinding noise or intermittent starting often means a failing starter or its solenoid, although a weak battery or poor connections cause similar symptoms.
Single loud click, grinding when starting, sometimes starts and sometimes doesn't, dashboard lights stay bright when you turn the key.
White, green or blue powder on battery terminals, or a loose clamp, can stop current flowing and cause slow cranking, clicking or no start even with a good battery.
Crusty powder on the terminals, flickering dashboard when starting, intermittent no-start.

Lights that flicker or pulse usually point to an unstable voltage from a failing alternator or regulator, a weak battery, or a loose or corroded connection, especially the battery or ground connections.
Lights pulse with engine speed, warning lights flicker, electrical items act strangely.
12 V socket or USB port not working
phone charger not working in car
ayaw mag charge ng phone sa kotse
When a 12 V socket or USB port stops working, a blown fuse is the most common cause, often after plugging in a faulty or high-power device. A coin or debris in the socket can also short it.
Socket and sometimes the radio or other items on the same fuse stop working together.
Car alarm going off by itself

An alarm that triggers on its own is usually caused by a weak battery (in the car or key fob), a door, bonnet or boot switch that doesn't register as closed, an over-sensitive shock sensor or a faulty aftermarket alarm.
Alarm sounds with no one near the car, the door-open light flickers, the alarm triggers in wind or rain.
Immobiliser or security light and key not recognised
