The immobiliser lets the engine run only with a recognised key. If the key isn't recognised, the security light flashes or stays on and the engine won't start or starts and dies after a second.
Security light on or flashing when trying to start, engine cranks but dies immediately, or won't crank.
When replacing a battery, use one with the specification the manual lists and connect it in the correct order. Some cars need settings relearned or a battery registration afterwards.
Nothing happens when trying to start

If nothing happens at all when you try to start, with no click and no dashboard lights, the most likely causes are a completely flat battery or a disconnected or corroded battery terminal. If the lights work but nothing happens, check the gear selector and clutch or brake pedal first.
No lights, no sound; or dashboard lights on but no click.
Glow plug (pre-heat) light on a diesel

On a diesel, the glow plug light (a coil symbol) comes on briefly at start-up while the glow plugs heat; wait for it to go out before cranking. If it flashes or stays on while driving, many diesels use it to warn of an engine-management fault.
Light that stays on or flashes while driving, hard cold starts, white smoke at start-up.
Service reminder or maintenance due light

A service or maintenance reminder (often a spanner symbol or 'MAINT REQD') is a timer, not a fault warning: it tells you a scheduled service is due. On some cars a spanner light can also mean a drivetrain fault, so check the manual.
Light or message appearing at a set distance or time since the last service reset.
Master warning light (triangle with exclamation mark)
A triangle with an exclamation mark is a master warning: it lights up together with a message or another warning to draw your attention. Read the message on the display to find out what it refers to.
Usually comes with a message on the instrument display.
Low washer fluid and washers not spraying
If the washers don't spray, the reservoir may be empty, the nozzles blocked or the pump or its fuse failed. Good washers matter for visibility in rain and dust.
Low washer warning, the pump hums but nothing sprays (blocked or empty), or no sound at all (pump or fuse).
Many warning lights on at once
several lights came on at once

When many warning lights come on together while driving, the cause is often a charging-system fault or low battery voltage, or a network fault between control modules, rather than many separate failures.
Battery, ABS, traction and other lights at the same time; gauges acting strangely.

The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust. A clogged converter restricts the exhaust, causing loss of power (especially uphill or at speed), heat under the car and a rotten-egg smell; broken internals can rattle.
Power loss that worsens with speed, glowing-hot converter, rotten-egg smell, rattle from under the car, P0420.

An exhaust that suddenly gets loud, rumbles or ticks usually has a hole, a cracked pipe, a failed gasket or a broken muffler. Exhaust leaks under the car can let fumes, including carbon monoxide, into the cabin.
Loud rumbling or roaring, ticking at cold start, exhaust smell inside the car, a hanging pipe.
Exhaust fumes smell inside the car

Exhaust fumes inside the car are dangerous because they contain carbon monoxide, which has no smell itself and causes headaches, dizziness and drowsiness. Common causes are an exhaust leak, a damaged tailpipe or poor door or boot seals.
Exhaust smell in the cabin, headache, dizziness or drowsiness while driving.

Failing an emissions test usually points to a fault that raises exhaust pollutants: misfires, a faulty oxygen sensor, a worn catalytic converter, a dirty air filter or, on diesels, smoke from injectors or air supply problems.
High emissions readings, visible smoke, a check-engine light.
Rattle from the exhaust heat shield
A thin metallic rattle from under the car, often at certain engine speeds or over bumps, is commonly a loose exhaust heat shield. It is usually harmless but annoying; check that nothing is dragging.
Tinny buzz or rattle at idle, at a particular rpm or over bumps.
Noise when the A/C is switched on

A grinding, rattling or squealing noise that starts when the A/C is switched on usually comes from the compressor, its clutch or the drive belt. A normal click when the compressor engages is expected.
Noise only with the A/C on, squeal at switch-on, rapid clicking on and off, reduced cooling.
Water dripping under the car from the A/C
Clear, odourless water dripping under the front of the car after using the A/C is normal condensation from the evaporator. If water drips inside onto the floor instead, the drain may be blocked.
Clear water with no smell or slipperiness under the front passenger area after A/C use.

Cabin heat comes from engine coolant passing through the heater core. A heater that blows cold usually means low coolant, a thermostat stuck open, a blocked heater core or a faulty blend door that won't move to hot.
Cold air even when the engine is warm, temperature gauge low, clicking behind the dashboard.
A/C or heater fan not blowing

If no air comes from the vents, the blower motor, its resistor or control module, a fuse or a relay has usually failed. A fan that works only on the highest speed almost always points to the blower resistor.
No airflow, only some speeds work, noise from behind the glovebox.
Engine starts then dies straight away

An engine that fires and dies within a second or two is often being stopped by the immobiliser (security light flashing), or isn't getting steady fuel or air: a weak fuel pump, a dirty throttle body or idle control, a vacuum leak or a failing sensor.
Security light flashing (immobiliser), or rough sputter before dying (fuel or air).
died in the middle of the road

An engine that cuts out while driving loses power steering and brake assistance, so steering and braking need much more effort. Common causes include fuel supply problems, a failing crankshaft sensor, an ignition fault or an alternator that has let the battery go flat.
Sudden cut-out, sometimes after a warning light, sputtering or when hot.
Whistling or wind noise while driving
A whistle or rushing noise that rises with speed usually comes from a worn door or window seal, a door that doesn't close fully, a roof rack or a loose trim piece.
Noise that rises with speed and changes with wind direction.
Clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse
A clunk when selecting Drive or Reverse usually comes from worn engine or transmission mounts, play in the driveline (CV joints, driveshaft U-joints or differential) or a high idle speed.
Single clunk when selecting a gear, sometimes when pulling away or lifting off the throttle.
A vibration that appears under acceleration and fades when coasting usually comes from the driveline: worn inner CV joints, a driveshaft or U-joint problem, or worn engine or transmission mounts.
Shudder or vibration under load, smooth when coasting; a check-engine light suggests a misfire instead.
A burning-oil smell after driving usually means oil is dripping onto hot exhaust parts from a leaking valve-cover gasket, oil filter, drain plug or seal, or was spilled during an oil change.
Oil smell or light smoke from under the hood after driving, oily patches on the engine or ground, falling oil level.

BLOWBAGETS is a common Philippine checklist for a quick check before a trip: Battery, Lights, Oil, Water (coolant), Brakes, Air (tire pressure), Gas (fuel), Engine, Tires and Self (the driver is fit and rested).
Preparing a car for a long road trip

Before a long trip, check the basics a few days ahead so there is time to fix anything: tires (pressure, tread and damage, including the spare), oil and coolant levels, brakes, lights and wipers, and that any service due is done.
Gear oil for the gearbox, differential and transfer case

Manual gearboxes, differentials and 4WD transfer cases use gear oil that also wears over time. Some are 'filled for life', others have intervals in the manual, and towing, off-road use and water crossings call for earlier checks.
Whine from the gearbox or axle, notchy shifting, leaks at seals.
Breaking in a new car or new engine

Many manufacturers recommend gentle driving for an initial period: varying speed, avoiding full-throttle acceleration, heavy towing and long periods at constant high speed. The details and distance are in the owner's manual.
Washing and caring for the paint

Regular washing removes dirt, salt, bird droppings and tree sap that damage paint. Wash in the shade with a car shampoo and a soft mitt, rinse well and dry with a clean cloth; wax or sealant adds protection.

Rust starts where paint is chipped or where mud and water collect. Washing the underside after floods and muddy roads, fixing paint chips early and keeping drain holes clear slow corrosion; structural rust needs a professional inspection.
Bubbling paint, orange stains at seams, holes in floor or sills.
How to check and set tire pressure

The correct tire pressure for your car is on a placard (usually inside the driver's door frame, fuel flap or glovebox) and in the owner's manual, not the maximum printed on the tire. Check it when tires are cold, monthly and before long trips.
Inspecting a used car before buying
what to check when buying a used car
bibili ng second hand na kotse
Before buying a used car, check the documents and service history, inspect it cold, test-drive it on different roads, and ideally have an independent mechanic inspect it and scan for trouble codes.
Inspecting a car after a collision or hitting a pothole

Even a minor collision, curb strike or deep pothole can damage tires, wheels, suspension, steering and alignment without obvious signs. Watch for new vibration, pulling, noises or warning lights, and have it inspected.
Pulling, steering wheel off-centre, vibration, bulges on the tire, warning lights, fluid leaks.
Simple monthly checks for car owners
A few minutes a month catches most problems early: tire pressure and condition, engine oil and coolant levels, brake and washer fluid, lights and wipers, and any new warning lights, noises or leaks.
After an accident in a rental car, make everyone safe first, then document the scene and report to the rental team and, where required, the police. Don't arrange repairs yourself.

If a rental car breaks down, get to safety, then contact the rental team with the location, what happened and any warning lights. They will arrange assistance; don't arrange repairs or towing yourself unless they ask you to.
Lost or damaged key for a rental car

If you lose or damage the key of a rental car, contact the rental team straight away. Keys with immobiliser chips or smart keys must be supplied or programmed by the dealer or the rental company; charges depend on the rental agreement.
Flat tire on a rental car

With a flat tire on a rental car, stop somewhere safe, switch on the hazard lights and contact the rental team. If you can change it safely, use the spare and tools supplied, then tell the rental team so the tire can be repaired or replaced.
Traffic violation or ticket with a rental car

Traffic violations and fines incurred during a rental are normally the renter's responsibility. Settle or report them as your rental agreement says and keep the ticket and receipt; some rental companies charge an admin fee for fines they receive later.
Warning light on a rental car
may ilaw sa dashboard ng rental

If a warning light comes on in a rental car, check what it is: red lights (brakes, oil pressure, temperature, battery) mean stop safely; yellow or orange lights mean have it checked soon. Contact the rental team with a photo of the dashboard.
Towing a car that has broken down

How a car may be towed depends on its drivetrain: many automatic, AWD and 4WD vehicles must be carried on a flatbed or with the drive wheels lifted, because towing with the driven wheels on the ground can damage the transmission. Check the owner's manual.
Car stuck in mud, sand or a ditch

If the car is stuck, spinning the wheels usually digs it deeper and can overheat the transmission or clutch. Straighten the wheels, clear around the tires, add traction under the driven wheels and use gentle throttle.

Hot weather is hard on batteries, tires, coolant and A/C. Keep coolant at the right level, check tire pressure when cold, park in shade or use a sunshade, and never leave children, pets or pressurised cans or lighters in a parked car.
